tutorials.title: C Programming: Think Like the Machine
tutorials.description: Learn C and see how memory really works. This is the base for systems, embedded and security work.
tutorials.content: C is close to the hardware, so you learn what the computer is really doing. You will write small programs in the terminal, use pointers, manage memory yourself and save data to a file. You need a computer with gcc (on Windows install MinGW or use WSL).

lessons.title: Your first C program
lessons.content: Every C program starts in a function called main. You write the code in a file that ends with .c, then compile it with gcc. Compiling turns your text into a program the computer can run. printf prints text, and return 0 tells the system that everything went well. Compile with: gcc hello.c -o hello -Wall and run it with ./hello (on Windows: hello.exe). The -Wall flag shows warnings, so always use it.

lessons.title: Variables, types and memory
lessons.content: A variable is a named place in memory. The type tells the computer how many bytes to use and how to read them. An int is usually 4 bytes, a char is 1 byte and a float is 4 bytes. The sizeof operator tells you the size. Knowing the size of your data is the first step to understanding memory.

lessons.title: Pointers
lessons.content: A pointer is a variable that holds the address of another variable. &score gives the address of score, and *p gives the value stored at the address in p. Pointers let a function change the real variable instead of a copy. This is how C functions return more than one result, and how arrays are passed around.

lessons.title: The heap: malloc and free
lessons.content: Local variables live on the stack and disappear when the function ends. When you need memory that lives longer, or whose size you only know while the program runs, you ask the heap with malloc. You must always check that malloc did not return NULL, and you must give the memory back with free. If you forget, you get a memory leak. Strings in C are just char arrays that end with a zero byte, written '\0'.

lessons.title: Saving data in files
lessons.content: Programs forget everything when they stop, unless you save to a file. fopen opens a file (modes: r read, w write, a add at the end). fprintf writes text, fgets reads a line, and fclose closes the file. Always check that fopen did not return NULL, because the file may be missing or locked.

tutorials.projectBrief: Build a command line Contact Book in C. The user can add a contact (name and phone), list all contacts, search by name, and quit. Keep the contacts in memory that you get with malloc, save them to a file when the program closes, and load them again when it starts. Put the code on GitHub with a README that explains how to compile and run it, then send the link.
rubric: Uses malloc and free correctly and checks for NULL
Add, list and search all work
Contacts are saved to a file and loaded again
Does not crash on empty or very long input
Code is split into small functions with clear names
README explains how to compile and run

tutorials.title: Web Basics: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
tutorials.description: Build and publish your first real website that works on a phone.
tutorials.content: You will learn the three building blocks of every website. HTML gives the structure, CSS gives the style and JavaScript makes the page react to the user. At the end you publish your site for free so anyone can open it. You only need a browser and a text editor like VS Code.

lessons.title: HTML: the structure of a page
lessons.content: HTML uses tags to describe the content. Headings (h1 to h6), paragraphs (p), links (a), images (img), lists (ul and li) and forms are the tags you will use most. Every page has a head with the title and a body with what people see. Save the file with the .html ending and open it in your browser.
lessons.code:
Welcome to my shop

We sell fresh fruit in Kigali.

Contact us

lessons.title: CSS: style and layout
lessons.content: CSS chooses elements with selectors and changes how they look: colours, fonts, spacing and the box model (content, padding, border, margin). Flexbox places items in a row or column and a media query changes the design on small screens. Most young people in Rwanda use a phone, so always check your page at phone width.

lessons.title: JavaScript: make it react
lessons.content: JavaScript runs in the browser. It can find an element with document.getElementById, listen for events like a click, and change the page. Start small: one button that changes one text. Then try reading what a user typed in a form and checking it before sending.

lessons.title: Git and publishing on GitHub Pages
lessons.content: Git saves versions of your project and GitHub stores them online. Make a repository, push your files, then in the repository settings turn on GitHub Pages. After a minute your site has a public link you can put on your CV. Make small commits with short messages that explain what changed.
lessons.code:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "first version of my shop page"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-NAME/my-shop.git
git push -u origin main

tutorials.projectBrief: Build a small website for a real or imaginary local business (a shop, a tutor, a salon). It needs at least three sections, a contact form that JavaScript checks before accepting (for example the name cannot be empty and the phone must have 10 digits), and a layout that looks good on a phone. Publish it with GitHub Pages and send the link to the live site and the repository.
rubric: The live site opens from the link
HTML is well structured with headings, links and a form
The layout works on a phone screen
JavaScript checks the form and shows a clear message
There are several commits with clear messages
The content is original and readable

tutorials.title: Python for Problem Solving
tutorials.description: Learn to think in steps and solve small real problems with Python.
tutorials.content: Python is a friendly language that is used for automation, data and the web. In this path you practise turning a problem into steps, and the steps into code. You need Python 3 installed, and you can run everything in the terminal.

lessons.title: Variables, input and output
lessons.content: A variable stores a value, like name or age. input() asks the user to type something and print() shows a result. Everything from input() is text, so use int() to turn it into a number before you calculate.
lessons.code:
name = input("What is your name? ")
age = int(input("How old are you? "))

print("Hello", name)
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.content: An if statement lets the program choose. A for loop repeats code, for example for every number in a range. Python uses indentation (spaces at the start of the line) to show which code belongs inside the if or the loop.

lessons.title: Lists and dictionaries
lessons.content: A list keeps many values in order, like marks. A dictionary keeps pairs, like a name and its mark. You can add to a list with append, count with len, and find the biggest value with max. These two are the tools you will use in almost every program.
lessons.code:
marks = [45, 70, 88, 52]
marks.append(91)
print(len(marks), "marks, highest is", max(marks))

student = {"name": "Alice", "mark": 88}
print(student["name"], "got", student["mark"])

lessons.title: Functions and files
lessons.content: A function is a block of code with a name that you can use again. It takes inputs and can return a result. To work with real data you read files with open(). The with statement closes the file for you when you are done.

tutorials.projectBrief: Build a Student Marks Analyser. The program reads marks from a CSV file (one student and mark per line), then prints the average, the highest and lowest mark with the student names, and how many students passed (50 or more). It must also write these results to a report.txt file. Handle a missing file and bad lines without crashing. Put it on GitHub with a sample marks file and a README, then send the link.
rubric: Average, highest, lowest and pass count are correct
Missing file or bad lines do not crash the program
README and a sample file are included
